books.section: Topic 6.6 The Rise of Industrial Capitalism
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904)

options.text: It turned public opinion against the trusts

options.misconception: Tarbell attacked Standard Oil’s methods, not private ownership itself.
options.text: It proved that all corporations should be owned by the government

options.misconception: Background: her work helped bring the Sherman Act to bear on Standard Oil, not end it.
options.text: It ended the Sherman Antitrust Act

options.misconception: Tarbell documented rebates and methods that courts later ruled unlawful.
options.text: It showed that Standard Oil had never broken any law

rationales.A: Background: Tarbell’s articles ran in McClure’s from 1902 to 1904 and became the classic exposé of a trust, arming the Progressive attack on the trusts.
rationales.B: Tarbell criticized how Standard Oil grew, not the idea of private business. Her remedy was exposure and law, not ownership.
rationales.C: Background: the Sherman Act was the tool used against Standard Oil in 1911. Tarbell’s work pointed toward using it, not ending it.
rationales.D: Background: the Supreme Court found in 1911 that Standard Oil violated the Sherman Act, the opposite of clearing the company.
rationales.general:
Ask what an exposé does.
1. Tarbell counts the profits of the combination in hard figures.
2. Background: her articles ran in a popular magazine and were read across the country.
3. Readers who had only suspected a monopoly now had names, figures, and methods.
4. That evidence fed the reformers who moved against the trusts.
Remember: an exposé matters when it gives reformers facts they can use.

stem: Why did Tarbell’s account of Standard Oil matter beyond the oil business?

stimulus.source_note: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company, Vol. 2, Chapter 18 (1904), public domain.
stimulus.text: “The profits of the present Standard Oil Company are enormous. For five years the dividends have been averaging about forty-five million dollars a year, or nearly fifty per cent. on its capitalisation, a sum which capitalised at five per cent. would give $900,000,000. Of course this is not all that the combination makes in a year. It allows an annual average of 5.77 per cent. for deficit, and it carries always an ample reserve fund.”
